rationale: The crude draw and the 6.9 mb total commercial draw look supportive, but the higher crude imports and flat distillate stocks mean the headline overstates US tightening.
Talk of a diesel export ban threatened USGC runs and therefore US crude demand, but this risk was overtaken by the 2 Oct decision to hold off.
Conflicting signals on a ban hit ULSD and refiner equities, but the effect on crude was ambiguous and has been superseded.
An intercepted Houthi strike set against reports of US-Iran talks created two-way headline risk, with Brent Nov falling on the deal talk.
The rejected Hormuz proposal pushes out any reopening and extends the Gulf supply constraint, which matters most for the Brent-linked market.
Middle East exports are still well below pre-war levels but appear to be recovering at the margin, easing the seaborne crude bottleneck; the figure is single-sourced from Kpler.
The SPR exchange could add sour barrels on the USGC in Nov-Dec, but uptake is uncertain given the weak take-up of the June offer.
The prior week's crude build came from lower runs while products drew, so it is now stale relative to the latest report.
Halting Chinese product exports removes Asian fuel supply and lifts cracks, which coincided with the week's largest Brent rally.
The G7 crude and diesel release adds policy supply, and with the diesel ban shelved, WTI fell on the day while Brent was flat.
OPEC+ quotas are non-binding, so the meeting matters less than Iran's stance keeping Hormuz closed, which supports Brent risk premia.
The STEO price path sits above the curve, but it is a forecast whose inputs predate the G7 release rather than a balance shock.
The surprise crude draw was export-led while Cushing built, the IEA is accelerating stock releases and the WTI prompt spread is near flat, so both benchmarks still fell on the week.
A fifth straight OPEC cut to 2026 demand growth confirms that demand destruction is visible even in OPEC's numbers.
OPEC's 2027 rebound treats 2026 losses as deferred demand, which has little bearing on the near-term balance.
A marginal revision to the call on OPEC+ crude does not bind while Gulf exports remain logistics-limited.
The higher 2027 call implies a later OPEC+ output rebuild if transit normalises, which is outside this week's horizon.
The August OPEC-12 output change comes from an unverified third-party summary and is too uncertain to weigh.
The IEA sees sharp demand contraction, leaving a wide gap with OPEC that highlights how uncertain the demand side is.
Large global stock draws point to a depleted buffer that supports structure, though the data are backward-looking.
The STEO's higher 4Q26 Brent forecast assumes constrained Middle East flows and excludes the G7 release.
The annual forecasts imply prices easing into 2027 but have no direct bearing on this week.
Middle East shut-ins easing from August corroborates the gradual recovery in Gulf flows.
The September pause is dated and was superseded by the October meeting.
A second pause is irrelevant while actual output is running below targets.
Chinese crude imports rose month on month but remain well below pre-war seaborne levels.
Higher Chinese refinery runs lift crude demand, but they are running ahead of available crude.
Ongoing draws on China's onshore stocks suggest import demand could recover once flows allow.
This export estimate sets the baseline for the suspension's impact, but definitions differ across sources.
China's PMI returning marginally above 50 is a mild positive for demand sentiment.
The indefinite export halt tightens Asian product balances and supports cracks and crude.
